theme: Table of nations; Babel and the scattering; Abram introduced
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 10:1-11:32. This is the longest single reading of Unit 2, but it moves quickly because much of it is genealogy. The two chapters fit together: chapter 10 lists the nations that descend from Noah’s three sons, chapter 11 explains why the nations are scattered and speak different languages. The reading ends with the introduction of Abram, setting up the next unit.
settingTheScene:
Yesterday we saw God establish the Noahic Covenant, a promise to preserve creation despite human sin. Today’s reading shows that human sin has not been reset, and the consequences continue to spread. Genesis 10-11 covers the transition from the post-flood world to the calling of Abram. It is the bridge between primeval history and patriarchal history.

These two chapters are a deliberate pair. Chapter 10 (the Table of Nations) lists seventy nations descended from Noah’s sons, a panoramic view of how the post-flood world filled up. Chapter 11 then circles back to explain how that scattering happened: the tower of Babel, where humanity’s pride attempted to make a name for itself and was scattered by God. The order is intentional, the result before the explanation, the consequence before the cause.
observation: Genesis 10 lists 70 nations descended from Noah’s three sons: Japheth (14), Ham (30), and Shem (26). Seventy will become a significant number throughout the Bible.
The list is theologically loaded, these are not just family trees but the world’s nations as God sees them.
Babel/Babylon (in the line of Cush) is highlighted in 10:8-10. The kingdom of Nimrod begins at Babel.
Genesis 11:1 makes a striking claim: “the whole earth had one language and the same words.” This is the situation before the scattering.
Humanity gathers on the plain of Shinar (the same region as Babel) and decides: “let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves.”
Note the verbs: “let us build… let us make a name.” Humanity attempts what only God can rightly do, establish itself and make a name.
God “comes down” to see the tower, language of divine condescension, perhaps with a hint of irony at humanity’s tiny achievement.
God confuses their language so they cannot understand one another. The result is the scattering of the nations.
Genesis 11:10-26 is the second post-flood genealogy, narrowing from all nations down to Shem’s line, all the way to Terah and Abram.
The reading ends with Terah’s family in Haran, and Abram set up for the great call that opens the next unit.
interpretation:
Genesis 10 and 11 belong together as a single theological unit. They tell us how the world we live in came to be, a world of many nations, many languages, scattered across the globe, and they tell us why. The two chapters together teach us about the unity and diversity of humanity, about the perennial human temptation to self-aggrandizement, and about how God’s redemptive plan narrows down to one family in preparation for the next stage of the story.

Genesis 10, sometimes called the Table of Nations, is unique in ancient literature. No other ancient civilization produced a document like it, a genealogical map of the entire known world, organized around three brothers and seventy descendants. The number seventy is significant. It will reappear in the seventy elders who go up with Moses (Exodus 24), the seventy who descend to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:27), and the seventy disciples Jesus sends out in Luke 10. The implication is that God’s view of “the nations” is comprehensive but not chaotic. There is order, even in a scattered world.

But Genesis 10 also contains a quiet hint of trouble. In verses 8-10, we are told that Nimrod, a descendant of Ham, became “a mighty hunter before the LORD,” and that “the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.” Babel, and the land of Shinar, will appear again in chapter 11 as the place where humanity organizes itself against God. Nimrod is the first empire-builder in the Bible, and his domain is the same domain that will become Babylon, the great archetypal enemy of God’s people throughout Scripture. The shadow is already falling.

Then chapter 11 explains how the scattering of the nations actually happened. Verse 1 sets the scene: “the whole earth had one language and the same words.” This is the pre-Babel world, unified, with shared communication. Then humanity migrates to the plain of Shinar and proposes a building project. The language is striking. “Let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves.” Three verbs in one sentence: let us build, let us make a name, lest we be dispersed. Each of these is a usurpation. Humanity is meant to be fruitful and multiply across the earth (Genesis 1:28; 9:1), but they are gathering in one place. Humanity is meant to receive a name from God (Adam was named by God; Eve was named by Adam, but in submission to God’s word), but they are making a name for themselves. Humanity is meant to fill the earth, but they are trying to avoid being dispersed.

The tower itself is a profound theological symbol. A tower “with its top in the heavens” is an assault on the boundary between heaven and earth. It is an attempt to ascend to where God dwells, on humanity’s own terms, by humanity’s own engineering. It is the sin of Eden in architectural form, “you will be like God”, repeated on a civilizational scale. And the motive is pride: “let us make a name for ourselves.” The reason God’s people make a name for themselves at all in Scripture is when God gives them a name. To make a name for yourself is to claim what only God can give.

God’s response is gracious irony. “And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower” (verse 5). The tower whose top was in the heavens is so small that God has to come down to see it. The pride of humanity is reduced to its true scale. And then God acts. He confuses their language, and they cannot understand one another, and the project collapses. Humanity is scattered across the face of the earth, which is what they were supposed to do all along.

But the chapter does not end in judgment. Verses 10-26 narrow the focus down. From all the nations of chapter 10, we are now tracing one line, Shem’s descendants. From Shem to Eber (whose name probably gives us “Hebrew”), from Eber to Peleg, all the way to Terah, who fathers Abram, Nahor, and Haran. The genealogy is selective and deliberate. The whole world has been mapped in chapter 10. The whole world has been scattered in chapter 11. And now the redemptive story is going to narrow to one man, Abram, through whom all the scattered nations of the earth will eventually be blessed.

This narrowing is not a contraction of God’s purposes. It is the strategy by which his purposes will reach all the nations. God will not save the world by addressing all nations equally. He will save the world by calling one man, forming one nation, fulfilling his promises through one descendant, who will then bring blessing back to all the families of the earth. The pattern is set here in Genesis 11 and will define the rest of the biblical story.
connection: Unit 2 has traced the trajectory of sin in the post-Eden, post-Fall world. Genesis 4 showed it in one family, Cain and Abel. Genesis 5 showed it as the universal experience of death across generations. Genesis 6-9 showed it overflowing into corruption, then judgment, then preserved by covenant. Today’s reading shows it on a civilizational scale, humanity united in rebellion at Babel, scattered by God, and yet through it all, the line of promise is preserved. The genealogy that ends Genesis 11 sets up Unit 3 perfectly: out of the scattered nations, God will call one man, Abram. Through him, the blessing will eventually come to “all the families of the earth” (Genesis 12:3). Pentecost in Acts 2 will be the great reversal of Babel, when the gospel is preached, the languages are heard, and the nations begin to come back to God through Christ.
application:
The temptation of Babel is not ancient. It is contemporary. “Let us build ourselves a city… and make a name for ourselves.” Humans still want to make a name for themselves. Still want to ascend to heaven on their own terms. Still want to gather in unified rebellion against the boundaries God has established. The names of the projects change. The technologies change. The slogans change. But the impulse is the same.

Examine your own ambitions today. What names are you trying to make for yourself? In your career, your relationships, your social presence, your accomplishments, where are you trying to ascend to a place where you can stand without need of God? The Christian life is not about achieving namelessness; it is about receiving the name God gives. Abram becomes Abraham. Jacob becomes Israel. Simon becomes Peter. Saul becomes Paul. And every believer is given the name of Christ. The name you are seeking is already being offered, freely. Let go of the tower.

There is also a positive application. The scattering of Babel was a judgment, but it was also a strategy. By dispersing humanity, God set up the long story by which the gospel would one day reach every nation. At Pentecost, the curse of Babel was beginning to be reversed, people from every nation under heaven heard the gospel in their own language. The Great Commission picks up where Babel left off: go to all the nations, baptize them, teach them. The diversity of the nations is not a problem to be undone; it is a stage on which the glory of God’s redemption can be displayed.

If you are part of a church today, you are part of the answer to Babel. The blood of Christ has begun to do what scattered languages could never undo, bring people together not into a single tower of pride but into a single body of grace. Pray for the gospel to keep doing this. And live in the awareness that your role, however small it feels, is part of the great reversal that began at Pentecost and will be consummated when the nations gather around the throne of the Lamb.
prayerPrompts: Confess any tower you have been building to make a name for yourself.
Ask him to help you rest in the name he gives you in Christ.
Pray for people from nations and languages that are not yours, that they would be gathered in.
